Lette.et: Ultimately from Latvian latvis. The e-vocalism might be generalized from the adjective lettisch (lättisch).

Letten.et: From Middle High German lette, from Old High German letto, from Proto-Germanic *ladjō-, from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂t- (“moist, wet”). Cognate with Icelandic leðja (“mud, muck”), Welsh llaid (“mire”), Lithuanian latakas (“gutter”), and possibly Latin latex.

Lettner.et: From Middle High German lettener, lecter, from Latin lectorium.

letzte.et: From Middle High German lest, a contraction of leȥȥest, from Old High German leȥȥist (also laȥȥōst), itself superlative of laȥ (cognate to English late). The modern German form with -tz- is of northern origin; two separate origins have probably met in it: Firs…

lettig.et: From Middle High German lettic, lettec, from Old High German lettīg. By surface analysis, Letten + -ig.

to terminate the relationship, to quit with, to say goodbye

letzen.et: From Middle High German letzen, from Old High German lezzen, from Proto-Germanic *latjaną.

letzter Strohhalm.et: Literally, “last straw”. From the idiom nach jedem Strohhalm greifen (“to use even the least promising options out of desperation”), which is equivalent to English a drowning man will clutch at a straw.
